It makes the locally optimal choice at each step, hoping to reach a global optimum

questions.explanation: A greedy algorithm commits to the best immediate option and never reconsiders. It is correct only when the problem has the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure.

questions.prompt: For the activity selection problem, the correct greedy strategy is to always pick the activity that:

options.text: Finishes earliest among the remaining compatible ones

questions.explanation: Choosing the earliest-finishing activity leaves the most room for the rest, and this can be proven optimal by an exchange argument. Shortest-duration or earliest-start strategies both fail on counterexamples.

questions.prompt: Why does the greedy coin-change algorithm (always take the largest coin) fail for some coin systems?

options.text: It requires the coins to be sorted descending
For non-canonical denominations it can use more coins than the true optimum
It cannot handle a coin of value 1

questions.explanation: With coins {1, 3, 4} making 6, greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins) but 3 + 3 uses only two. Standard currency systems are designed so greedy happens to be optimal, but not all are.

questions.prompt: Huffman coding builds an optimal prefix code by greedily:

options.text: Merging the two lowest-frequency nodes repeatedly
Assigning fixed-length codes to all symbols

questions.explanation: Combining the two rarest symbols first pushes them deepest in the tree, giving them the longest codes. This local choice provably yields the minimum total encoded length.

questions.prompt: What two properties must a problem have for a greedy algorithm to be provably correct?

options.text: A sorted input and no duplicates
The greedy-choice property and optimal substructure

questions.explanation: The greedy-choice property means a locally optimal choice is part of some global optimum, and optimal substructure means the rest of the problem is solved the same way. Without both, greedy can be wrong.

questions.prompt: The fractional knapsack problem is solved optimally by greedily choosing items in order of:
questions.explanation: Because items can be split, filling the knapsack with the densest value first is optimal. The 0/1 version, where items cannot be split, is not solvable this way and needs dynamic programming.

questions.prompt: How is a greedy algorithm typically proven correct?

options.text: By running it on all inputs
By comparing it to brute force on small cases
By an exchange argument showing the greedy choice is no worse than any other

questions.explanation: An exchange argument shows any optimal solution can be transformed to include the greedy choice without becoming worse. This establishes correctness for all inputs, which testing cannot.

questions.prompt: Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm is greedy in that it repeatedly:

options.text: Finalises the unvisited vertex with the smallest tentative distance
Chooses the vertex with the most edges

questions.explanation: It greedily locks in the closest remaining vertex, knowing no shorter path to it can exist given non-negative weights. That assumption is exactly why Dijkstra fails on negative edges.

questions.prompt: For a set of jobs each with a deadline and a penalty for lateness, a common greedy scheduling rule is to:

options.text: Schedule jobs by earliest deadline first

questions.explanation: Earliest-deadline-first minimises maximum lateness for single-machine scheduling. Interval and scheduling problems frequently reduce to sorting by an endpoint and greedily selecting.

questions.prompt: Why can a greedy algorithm fail on the 0/1 knapsack problem?

options.text: Committing to the densest item may block a better combination that a whole-item constraint requires
Items cannot be compared by ratio

questions.explanation: Without the ability to take a fraction, the locally best ratio can leave capacity that a different, less dense set would have filled more valuably. The problem lacks the greedy-choice property, so DP is needed.
